# Business-Model Transition: Perpetual Licence to Subscription
## Offer Architecture, Migration Economics, Sales and Channel Compensation, Trough Governance

**Version 2.0 — complete for decision.** For the Board.
Circulated in advance to: CEO; CFO; **Treasurer**; Chief Revenue Officer; Chief Product Officer; **Chief Customer Officer / Head of Renewals**; General Counsel; Chief Accounting Officer; **CIO / Head of Business Systems (billing, CPQ, entitlement)**; VP Investor Relations; Head of Partner & Channel; **Chair, Compensation Committee**; **Chair, Audit Committee**.
Not yet for customer, employee, partner, analyst or market communication (§12.6, §14).

*Prior to Board circulation, the substance of §§6, 9 and 10 has been walked through individually with the CRO, the Head of Partner & Channel and the Chief Customer Officer, and the substance of §§4 and 11 with the CAO and Treasurer. Where their views differ from ours, we have recorded the difference rather than resolved it (§16.3). We would not wish the Board to discover a disagreement in the room that could have been surfaced on paper.*

---

### How to read this pack

Four notes, then the substance.

**On what this is not.** This is not a pricing exercise with a communications annexe attached. The documented failure pattern in this category is a company that redesigns its price book while leaving its compensation plan, its billing stack, its board scorecard and its investor narrative on the old model — and discovers six quarters later that every part of the organisation is still paid, measured and praised for selling the thing it has publicly stopped selling. Nor is it a request for more time. The direction has been decided by leadership [F]; our task is to specify it. Every design choice below is **named**; only the calibration is pending, and §15 says precisely which data sets it.

**On numbers, and on the existing model.** We have been shown leadership's transition model, which projects a multi-year revenue trough [F]. We regard it as soundly constructed and we have not rebuilt it. We would, respectfully, test six of its inputs (§3); on three we think the model is likely to be wrong, and we say in which direction. Beyond that model, illustrative values are used solely to show how the arithmetic behaves and are marked *[illus.]*. They carry no evidential weight and should not be quoted outside this room. Where a figure matters to a decision requested in §16, it appears in §15 with a named owner and a delivery date.

**On sequencing.** There is a natural instinct to defer the irreversible decisions until the reversible ones have been proved. It is a reasonable instinct and it is, we think, the trap. The longest-lead items — billing and entitlement systems, the auditor's revenue-recognition position, debt covenants, and the Board's own incentive metrics — are exactly the ones that feel least urgent and take longest to move. They sit in **Phase 0** (§11) for that reason. *A transition announced before its plumbing exists announces its own failure on a nine-month delay.*

**On consultation.** Two of the four constituencies affected by this plan — the field sales organisation and the long-standing installed base — will experience it as something being taken away. Our strong view is that neither should learn the shape of it from a company-wide announcement. §9.7 and §6.7 set out a deliberate sequence of small-group soundings, advisory-council testing and named-sponsor conversations *before* publication. This adds roughly five weeks to the calendar. We think it is the cheapest insurance in the pack, and it is the principal difference between our plan and what the comparator appears to have done (§2).

**Evidence markers.**
**[F]** fact stated in the brief. **[M]** figure or assumption drawn from leadership's existing transition model. **[P]** publicly documented comparator transition — directional only, to be verified by IR before any external use. **[A]** assumption, pending the data in §15. **[J]** our judgement, argued in the text and open to challenge.

---

## 1. Recommendation on a page

**Adopt a three-year "Balanced" transition. Do not force conversion; make staying more expensive than moving, slowly and predictably. Use an on-premise term licence as the deliberate trough-shaping instrument, not as a compromise. Price the entry conversion at parity with today's maintenance and buy the customer's consent with a three-year price-certainty window and a capped uplift thereafter. Pay the sales force on total contracted value with a declining transition multiplier and four quarters of protected earnings, and replace the channel's upfront margin before, not after, partners discover it has gone. Move the plumbing, the auditor position, the covenants and the Board's own comp metrics in Phase 0. Then pre-publish the trough — floor quarter, depth and recovery quarter — and be judged against a scorecard we choose, disclose and never quietly change.**

| | Recommendation |
|---|---|
| **Direction** | Subscription-first, but **not SaaS-only**. Three deployment forms sold from one price book: Cloud (ratable), **Term Licence on-premise** (partially recognised at delivery), Perpetual (closed to new customers at Month 12; available to existing base only by exception until Month 24) (§4, §5) |
| **The single largest trough lever** | Revenue recognition, treated as a **design variable, not plumbing.** Directing an [illus.] 35–45% of on-premise subscription bookings to term licence rather than hosted can materially reduce reported-revenue trough depth while building the same recurring commitment (§4.3) [J][A] |
| **Offer tiers** | Three editions — **Essential / Professional / Enterprise** — replacing the perpetual-plus-maintenance SKU sprawl. Enterprise carries the entitlements the top decile actually buys support for (§5.2) |
| **Headline price ratio** | Like-for-like Cloud subscription at **1.30–1.45 × current annual maintenance** for *new* customers; **1.00 × current maintenance for the first three years** for existing licence holders who convert in the Early Window (§6.2, §7.2) *[illus., calibrated by §15 items 3, 5, 9]* |
| **Migration ladder** | Four rungs, price rising and terms tightening at each: **Early Window (Months 1–12) → Standard Window (13–24) → Late Window (25–36) → Support Sunset.** No retrospective removal of perpetual rights, ever (§6) |
| **Trade-in credit** | Residual-value credit on the customer's declining unamortised licence value, applied against first-year subscription, capped and expiring with the Early Window (§6.3) |
| **The entitlement principle, stated plainly** | Perpetual licences are irrevocable property and we will say so publicly and without qualification. **Support, updates and cloud services are renewable and, with notice, sunsettable.** That distinction is the whole of the migration economics and must be handled as a relationship matter before it is a contract matter (§6.1) |
| **Support sunset** | Announced at Month 0, effective **Month 36** for new-version entitlement and **Month 48** for security-only support, with a priced Extended Support tier at 1.5× legacy maintenance for those who genuinely cannot move. Contractual notice periods verified per-contract by GC before announcement (§6.5) |
| **Sales compensation** | **TCV crediting with a transition multiplier declining 1.6× → 1.3× → 1.0× over three years**; ratable quota retirement; **four quarters of protected earnings at 90% of trailing-eight-quarter average**; migration-specific SPIFF; 12-month churn clawback; quota and territory reset published only after the soundings in §9.7 (§9) |
| **Channel** | Upfront VAR margin is structurally destroyed by subscription and partners will resist accordingly [J]. Replace with a **front-loaded first-year margin (higher than the old licence margin in year 1), a declining renewal annuity margin, a migration bounty per converted seat, and deal-registration protection extended to renewals** (§10) |
| **Trough shape, recommended scenario** | Balanced: revenue trough floor in **Q6–Q7**, depth **[illus.] 11–14%** below the Month-0 run-rate, recovery to prior peak by **Q11–Q13**; cash trough shallower and earlier than the revenue trough because of annual-upfront billing (§7.4, §8) [M][A] |
| **The two troughs** | **Revenue trough and cash trough are different animals with different remedies.** Cash is managed with annual-upfront billing as default, multi-year prepay discounts, and RPO build; revenue is managed with mix (term licence) and pace. Investors discount them differently and we will disclose them separately (§8) |
| **Investor architecture** | Metric switch to **ARR, cRPO, gross and net retention, cohort conversion rate, billings**; guidance **re-based to a three-year framework, not suspended**; trough floor and recovery quarter **pre-committed and published**; Analyst Day at Month 3 with cohort disclosure; covenant amendment **completed before announcement**; buyback used as a floor, not a rescue (§12) |
| **Board's own metrics** | The Compensation Committee must re-cut executive metrics **before** the announcement. We are otherwise asking the executive team to depress, deliberately and for three years, the numbers on which it is paid. This is a Phase 0 item, not a year-end item (§11.5) |
| **Governance** | **Dual operating model.** Perpetual run-off and subscription new business managed, forecast and reported separately, with a named **Transition Office** lead reporting to the CEO and dotted to the CFO, appointed within 15 days. The CRO cannot both hit this year's licence number and dismantle it [J] (§13) |
| **Adjust triggers, not abort triggers** | We do not recommend an abort trigger; a publicly reversed transition is worse than either state. We recommend **three pace-adjustment triggers** on gross retention, top-decile conversion and cash (§14.3) |
| **Decisions requested** | **Six**, listed in §16, sought at the Board meeting on **[date]** |

### 1.1 Our posture, said once and plainly

Two things deserve saying before the detail.

First: **the comparator's loss of a fifth of its installed base is the most valuable piece of information we have** [F], and it is the design constraint for everything that follows. Our reading — offered for testing, not for adoption — is that abrupt transitions do not fail on price. They fail because **optionality is withdrawn without notice**, which converts a pricing conversation into a dignity conversation, and dignity conversations are lost by vendors. A customer who is told "your choice is gone" will look at competitors, third-party support providers and version-freeze even when the economics of staying are better. §2 sets out how to size this before we design against it.

Second: **20% base loss is not automatically a failure, and 0% base loss is not automatically a success.** The relevant test is asymmetric (§2.3). Losing a fifth of the *seat* count at a materially higher revenue per retained customer may be value-accretive. Losing a fifth of the *top decile* — the reference customers, the multi-site accounts, the ones whose logos carry the analyst narrative — is not recoverable in this decade. We therefore recommend that the plan be tuned to protect the top decile almost regardless of cost, and be considerably more relaxed about the long tail, where a partner-led or self-serve motion may serve better than we do.

We would also ask that the transition be described internally, consistently and from the first day, as something the company is doing **with** its customers and its sales force rather than **to** them. If people believe otherwise, we will spend the trough managing defections rather than conversions, and the pace-adjustment triggers in §14.3 will all fire at once.

---

## 2. The comparator's 20%: decomposition before design

### 2.1 What we need to know, and how to know it

We should not design against a headline. Before the Month-3 gate we should decompose the comparator's loss from public sources and channel intelligence [P], accepting that the picture will be partial.

| Question | Why it changes our design |
|---|---|
| **Which segments left?** Small/tail, mid-market, or enterprise? | If tail-heavy, our tail can be moved to a partner-led motion and our own risk is lower than the headline. If enterprise-heavy, the Early Window incentives in §6.2 must be materially richer |
| **What ARR left, versus what seat count?** | Distinguishes a revenue event from a logo event. The two require different investor framing (§12.4) |
| **Where did they go?** Competitor / third-party support / version freeze / in-house | Version freeze is recoverable over 3–5 years; competitor migration usually is not. Third-party support tells us our support-sunset schedule is the exposed flank (§6.5) |
| **What notice was given on support entitlements?** | The variable we most suspect [J]. If notice was under 12 months, our 36/48-month schedule is our principal differentiator |
| **Was there any price-certainty commitment?** | If not, this is where we buy consent most cheaply (§6.2) |
| **Was the price increase concurrent with the model change?** | Combining a model change with a price rise merges two conversations and loses both [J]. We recommend explicit separation (§7.5) |

### 2.2 Our working hypothesis

Our hypothesis — marked as such — is that the comparator combined (a) a short support-sunset notice, (b) no price-certainty window, (c) a de facto price increase presented as a model change, and (d) a sales force still paid on upfront value, which meant the field quietly advised its best accounts to buy perpetual before the door closed and then had no relationship credit left when it did [J]. Each of those four is separately avoidable. §§6, 7 and 9 avoid them in that order.

### 2.3 The asymmetry test — to be run before Board approval of pace

For each decile of the installed base by ARR, we compute:

**Value at risk (decile) = ARR(decile) × P(defection | scenario) × [multiple applied to recurring revenue] − ARR(decile) × conversion uplift × P(conversion) × [same multiple]**

The output is a single page: which deciles we should protect at almost any cost, which we should convert at standard terms, and which we should be willing to lose. We recommend the pace in §7 be set by the **top three deciles only**. Managing the transition to the average customer is how the average is achieved and the important customers are lost [J].

*Owner: CFO with Chief Customer Officer. Due: §15 item 1.*

---

## 3. Six assumptions in the existing model, respectfully tested

The model is well built and we have not duplicated it. We would ask that six inputs be re-examined; on three we believe the current setting is optimistic or pessimistic in a knowable direction.

| # | Assumption in the model [M] | Our view | Direction of error | Effect if we are right |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Conversion is voluntary and price-elastic, with a single blended conversion curve | Conversion behaviour is bimodal, not blended: large accounts convert on **budget cycle and audit exposure**, tail accounts on **price**. One curve averages two behaviours that need two offers | Understates achievable enterprise conversion; overstates tail conversion | Trough shallower but longer; enterprise incentives can be cheaper than modelled |
| 2 | 100% of on-premise subscription revenue recognised ratably | Term-licence structures allow a material portion at delivery, subject to auditor pre-clearance | **Materially overstates trough depth** | Directionally, the largest single correction available (§4.3) |
| 3 | Maintenance attrition continues at the historic base rate | Attrition **rises** during any announced transition, in every comparator we can see [P] | Understates trough depth | Partly offsets #2; the two should be modelled together, not separately |
| 4 | Sales productivity constant through the change | Productivity falls for 2–4 quarter…[truncated]
